# The research wrote each life in its own words from the Wikipedia article and a second reference. It copied no sentence.

text: Fourth Almohad caliph from 1199, Muhammad al-Nasir inherited a vast empire from his father al-Mansur, the victor of Alarcos. He took Majorca from the Banu Ghaniya and won back Ifriqiya, leaving it under the governor whose line became the Hafsids. His invasion of Castile ended in disaster at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212, and legend tells of slaves chained around his tent there.

Abu Said Uthman ibn Jami came from a family of Andalusi administrators who served the Almohad court in Marrakesh. He was vizier to the caliph Muhammad al-Nasir from about 1205 and steered much of the daily business of the empire. After the defeat at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212 he helped arrange the succession of the next caliph, but he later lost power and was killed in exile.

Abd al-Wahid was a son of Abu Hafs Umar, the Hintata chief who had been one of Ibn Tumart's first companions. A leading Almohad general, he defeated enemy forces in a battle in October 1205, and in 1207 the caliph left him in Tunis as governor of Ifriqiya with unusually wide powers. A steady and trusted frontier lord, he founded the Hafsid line that would later rule Tunisia for three centuries and died on 25 February 1221.

Abd al-Wahid al-Marrakushi was born in Marrakesh in 1185 and studied in Fez and in al-Andalus, mixing with scholars close to the Almohad court. Around 1200 he was a young student of law and letters. Later he travelled east and finished al-Mujib, a history of the Maghreb, in 1224, a work lively with personal anecdote and frank judgements of the caliphs.

Yahya ibn Ishaq ibn Ghaniya led the Banu Ghaniya, the last Almoravid loyalists, who had sailed from Majorca to wage war on the Almohads in Ifriqiya. Taking command around 1188 after his brother Ali died, he seized Mahdia and on 14 December 1203 Tunis itself. Defeated in 1205, he never gave up, raiding from the desert edges for more than thirty years and earning a name as the most stubborn rebel of the Maghreb.

Sharaf al-Din Qaraqush was a mamluk of Armenian origin who served Saladin's nephew Taqi al-Din and was sent west in the early 1170s. He carved out a domain around Tripoli and the Tunisian Jarid and fought the Almohads. He allied with the Banu Ghaniya but was not a member of that family. He quarreled with Yahya ibn Ghaniya and was defeated and executed by him in 1212.

Al-Adil, known to the crusaders as Saphadin, was Saladin's younger brother and his most capable administrator and envoy. He negotiated with Richard the Lionheart during the Third Crusade, and after Saladin's death he patiently outplayed his quarrelling nephews, becoming sultan of Egypt and Syria in 1200. A shrewd and cautious diplomat, he ruled through his sons, whom he placed over Egypt, Damascus and the Jazira.

Al-Kamil was a son of al-Adil, who made him viceroy of Egypt in 1200. Sultan from 1218, he beat the Fifth Crusade at Damietta, and in 1229 he handed Jerusalem to Frederick II by treaty rather than fight a new war. Pragmatic and intellectually curious, he enjoyed debate with scholars, corresponded with the emperor on science, and famously received Francis of Assisi in his camp.

Al-Muazzam Isa was a son of al-Adil who governed Damascus for his father and ruled it in his own right from 1218 to 1227. A tough campaigner against the Franks, he had the walls of Jerusalem pulled down in 1219 so that crusaders could not use the city as a fortress. Unusually for a prince, he was a serious Hanafi jurist and grammarian who loved learned company and disliked courtly pomp.

Al-Ashraf Musa was a son of al-Adil who received Harran in 1201 and built up a large domain in the Jazira, with Akhlat near Lake Van among his holdings. From 1229 until his death in 1237 he ruled Damascus. Generous, cheerful and fond of music and pleasant company, he was among the best-liked Ayyubid princes, and he spent freely on mosques and schools.

Alexios III Angelos seized the Byzantine throne in 1195 by blinding and jailing his own brother Isaac II. His reign was marked by court extravagance, sold offices and shrinking defences. When the Fourth Crusade attacked in 1203 he fled Constantinople by night with a daughter and part of the treasury, then spent his last years plotting against his son-in-law Theodore Laskaris until he was shut in a monastery at Nicaea.

Alexios Doukas, nicknamed Mourtzouphlos for his heavy, joined eyebrows, was a Byzantine noble at the court of Alexios III around 1200. In early 1204 he overthrew and strangled the young Alexios IV and took the throne himself. He led the defence against the crusaders with real vigour, but after the city fell he was blinded by Alexios III, captured by the Latins and thrown to his death from a column in Constantinople.

Theodore Laskaris married Anna, daughter of Alexios III, in 1200 and soon held the rank of despot. After the crusaders took Constantinople in 1204 he escaped to Asia Minor, rallied the Greeks of Bithynia and made Nicaea the seat of a Byzantine government in exile, crowned emperor in 1208. Small in stature but daring, he reportedly faced the Seljuk sultan in person at the battle of Antioch on the Meander in 1211.

Niketas Choniates was a senior official of the Byzantine court, serving as grand logothete under the Angeloi. He saw the crusaders sack Constantinople in 1204, escaped with his family thanks to a Venetian friend, and settled at Nicaea. His History, covering 1118 to 1207, is the great eyewitness account of the empire's fall, written with irony, moral outrage and sharp portraits of the emperors he had served.

Michael Choniates, elder brother of the historian Niketas, was archbishop of Athens from about 1182. He held the Acropolis against the local strongman Leo Sgouros, then gave the city up to the crusaders in 1205 and withdrew into exile on the island of Kea. A refined scholar who owned rare classical texts, he wrote letters and poems lamenting how far Athens had fallen from its ancient glory.

Kaloyan, youngest brother of the founders of the restored Bulgarian state, became sole tsar in 1197. He took Varna from the Byzantines in 1201, won a crown from Pope Innocent III in 1204, and in 1205 crushed the crusaders at Adrianople, capturing the Latin emperor Baldwin. Ruthless toward his enemies, he styled himself the Roman-slayer, and he died in mysterious circumstances while besieging Thessalonica in 1207.

Boril was a nephew of Kaloyan and a young member of the ruling Asen family around 1200. When Kaloyan died in 1207 he married the tsar's Cuman widow and took the throne, but rival kinsmen never accepted him. He lost battles to the Latin emperor Henry, called a church council against the Bogomil heretics in 1211, and was finally overthrown and blinded by his cousin Ivan Asen II in 1218.

Strez was a kinsman of the Asen tsars and held the rank of sebastokrator. Refusing to accept Boril as tsar in 1207, he fled to Serbia and with Serbian help made himself master of the lands between the Struma and the Vardar from his fortress at Prosek. He later switched sides against his Serbian patrons, and Serbian church writers portrayed him as a cruel tyrant before his sudden death in 1214.

Rukn al-Din Suleiman II was a son of Kilij Arslan II who ousted his brother Kaykhusraw I in 1196 and reunited the Seljuk sultanate of Rum. Around 1200 he was the strongest ruler in Anatolia, taking Malatya and Erzurum and pressing the Byzantines. An energetic and ambitious sultan, he overreached when he invaded Georgia and was routed at Basian, and he died in 1204 soon after.

Izz al-Din Kaykaus was born in 1187, the eldest son of Kaykhusraw I. While his father was in exile his uncle Suleiman II ruled, and Kaykaus was still a boy in 1200. He became sultan of Rum in 1211, took the Black Sea port of Sinop in 1214, recovered Antalya on the Mediterranean, and opened Anatolian trade routes. A patron of learning, he founded a great hospital at Sivas, where he chose to be buried, and he died in 1220.

Frederick II, son of Henry VI and Constance of Sicily, was born at Jesi in 1194 and crowned king of Sicily as a small child in 1198. Around 1200 he was an orphan in Palermo, a ward of Pope Innocent III fought over by German captains and Sicilian barons. He grew into a brilliant, restless emperor who spoke several languages, wrote on falconry and was called the wonder of the world.

Markward of Annweiler was an imperial ministerial who rose to be seneschal of Henry VI and margrave of Ancona. After Henry's death he claimed the regency of Sicily for the young Frederick and fought the pope's men across the kingdom. Innocent III called him another Saladin and preached a crusade against him. A hard and capable soldier, he fell ill and died in September 1202 at Patti.

Walter of Palearia was bishop of Troia and chancellor of the Kingdom of Sicily under Henry VI and Constance. During the minority of Frederick II he was a leading member of the regency council, bargaining in turn with the pope, Markward of Annweiler and other German captains. A slippery and ambitious prelate, he became bishop of Catania in 1208 but later fell from favour with the young king.

Diepold of Schweinspeunt was a Bavarian ministerial whom Henry VI made count of Acerra in southern Italy. After 1197 he fought on for himself and the Hohenstaufen cause, killing Walter of Brienne in an ambush at Sarno in June 1205 and later contending for Palermo and the boy king. Otto IV made him duke of Spoleto in 1209. A tireless raider, he left a trail of sacked towns recorded by Richard of San Germano.

Leopold VI of the Babenberg family became duke of Styria in 1194 and of Austria in 1198. He sided with Philip of Swabia, went on crusade in Spain and at Damietta, and grew rich on the Danube trade through Vienna. Known as the Glorious, he kept a brilliant court where minnesingers such as Walther von der Vogelweide performed, and he was trusted as a peacemaker between emperor and pope.

Hadmar II of Kuenring was a powerful Austrian ministerial and the jailer of Richard the Lionheart at Durnstein castle in 1192 and 1193. Around 1200 he was one of the chief lords of the Babenberg duke, founding the town of Weitra and generously endowing Zwettl Abbey. Remembered both as a pious founder and as the head of a proud, unruly clan, he died in 1217 while on crusade.

Eldest son of Béla III, Emeric ruled Hungary and Croatia from 1196 and spent most of his reign fighting the revolts of his younger brother Andrew. He worked with Pope Innocent III against the Bosnian heretics, pushed Hungarian overlordship into Serbia, and could not stop Venice and the crusaders from taking Zadar in 1202. In 1203 he walked unarmed into Andrew's camp at Varaždin and arrested him without a blow being struck.

The restless younger son of Béla III, Andrew forced his brother King Emeric to grant him Croatia and Dalmatia in 1197 and kept plotting against him until he was seized in 1203. He took the throne in 1205 after the early death of his nephew Ladislaus III. Later known for lavish grants of royal land, the crusade of 1217 and the Golden Bull of 1222, he was a generous but erratic ruler who gave away more than his crown could afford.

Job was Archbishop of Esztergom, head of the Hungarian church, from 1185. Educated in Paris, he served Béla III as a diplomat, helped find the king a French bride and rebuilt Esztergom cathedral in the new Gothic style. Under Emeric he kept aloof from the feud between the king and Duke Andrew, which earned him royal distrust and a bitter rivalry with the see of Kalocsa. He once debated theology face to face with the Byzantine emperor Isaac II.

Born Lotario dei Conti di Segni, Innocent III became pope in 1198 at about 37 and was the most powerful pontiff of the Middle Ages. He claimed authority over all Christian kings, used interdicts to bend rulers such as Philip II of France and King John, launched the Fourth Crusade and the Albigensian Crusade, and crowned his work with the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215. Brilliant, legalistic and tireless, he saw himself as Christ's vicar set above nations.

Riccardo was the elder brother of Pope Innocent III and the chief winner from his nepotism. With papal backing he gathered castles and estates in Latium, and the huge Torre dei Conti in Rome is linked to his family. In 1208 his brother invested him with the county of Sora on the Sicilian border, taken from imperial partisans. A grasping baron rather than a churchman, he made the Conti a lasting power in Roman politics.

Peter of Capua, of a noble family of Amalfi, was a Paris-trained theologian and a cardinal from February 1193. As papal legate in France he laid the kingdom under interdict in January 1200 to force Philip II back to his rejected wife Ingeborg. He then served as legate to the Fourth Crusade and the Latin East, and he brought the relics of Saint Andrew from Constantinople to Amalfi, where the cathedral received them on 8 May 1208. He was admired as a brilliant preacher and scholar.

Ugolino dei Conti, a kinsman of Innocent III, was made a cardinal in 1198 and became one of the curia's sharpest lawyers and diplomats. He was the friend and protector of Francis of Assisi and helped shape the Franciscan rule. Elected pope as Gregory IX in 1227, already very old, he issued the Decretals, set up the papal Inquisition and fought the emperor Frederick II, whom he excommunicated more than once. He was famed for his iron will.

Enrico Dandolo was elected doge of Venice in 1192 when already in his eighties and nearly blind. He struck the bargain that bent the Fourth Crusade to Venice's profit, used the crusaders to retake Zadar in 1202, and led the assault on Constantinople in 1204, standing armed at the prow of his galley under the banner of Saint Mark. Shrewd, pious and amazingly vigorous for his age, he died in Constantinople in 1205 and was buried in Hagia Sophia.

Ranieri was the son of Doge Enrico Dandolo and governed Venice as vice-doge while his father was away on the Fourth Crusade. After the conquest he worked to secure Venice's share of the Byzantine lands, above all Crete, which the Genoese privateer Enrico Pescatore had seized. He led the first Venetian attack on the island in 1207 and was killed in the long war with Genoa for Crete. His daughter Anna later married the Serbian ruler Stefan Nemanjić.

Pietro Ziani, son of the rich doge Sebastiano Ziani, had been a sea captain in his youth and belonged to one of the wealthiest families in Venice. He took part in the Fourth Crusade and was elected doge in 1205 after Enrico Dandolo's death. He organised Venice's new holdings in Crete, Corfu and Constantinople, made treaties with Greek rulers and fought off Padua. Calm and businesslike, he gave up the office in 1229 and died soon after.

Tommaso Morosini, a Venetian noble cleric who was still only a subdeacon, was chosen by the Venetian clergy of Hagia Sophia as the first Latin Patriarch of Constantinople in 1204. Innocent III first condemned the election as uncanonical, then confirmed him and had him ordained priest and bishop in quick order. As patriarch he was accused of filling posts with Venetians and quarrelled with the emperor, French clergy and papal legates until his death in 1211.

Moses ben Maimon was born in Córdoba, left Spain with his family to escape Almohad persecution and settled in Egypt, where he led the Jewish community. The foremost rabbinic scholar of his age, he wrote the law code Mishneh Torah and the Guide for the Perplexed, which sought to reconcile faith with Aristotle. He also served as a physician at Saladin's court. Around 1200 he was old and overworked but still writing medical treatises; he died in 1204.

Kaykhusraw, youngest son of Kilij Arslan II, became Seljuk sultan of Rum in 1192 but was driven out by his brother Suleiman II in 1196. In 1200 he was an exile in Constantinople among the Byzantine nobility, and he married a daughter of the Greek magnate Manuel Maurozomes. He regained Konya in 1205, seized the port of Antalya in 1207 and fell in battle against Nicaea in 1211. Educated in four languages, he wrote poetry in Persian.

Leo Sgouros inherited the governorship of Nauplia around 1198 and, as Byzantine authority collapsed, made himself independent lord of Argos, Corinth and much of central Greece. He married a daughter of the fallen emperor Alexios III and took the title of despot. Notoriously violent, he invited the bishop of Corinth to dinner, had him blinded and thrown to his death from the heights. Besieged on the Acrocorinth by the crusaders, he took his own life in 1208.

Boniface, Marquis of Montferrat, was a veteran soldier and a generous patron of troubadours, chosen leader of the Fourth Crusade in 1201. Passed over for the imperial crown in 1204, he took Thessalonica and central Greece as his kingdom instead, driving out Leo Sgouros. He was killed in 1207 in a Bulgarian ambush in the Rhodope mountains, and his head was sent to Tsar Kaloyan. Courtly, ambitious and brave, he was praised in the songs of Raimbaut de Vaqueiras.

Francis was the pleasure-loving son of a rich cloth merchant of Assisi; in 1202 he fought for his city against Perugia and spent a year as a prisoner. Illness and spiritual crises turned him to radical poverty. He rebuilt ruined chapels, cared for lepers and gathered brothers whose way of life Innocent III approved around 1209. Joyful, gentle and theatrical, he preached to birds and in 1223 staged the first Christmas crib at Greccio, and was said to bear the stigmata.

Walter III, Count of Brienne in Champagne, married Elvira, daughter of the late King Tancred of Sicily, and set out to win her inheritance. Backed by Innocent III, he entered southern Italy in 1201 with a small army, won battles at Capua and Cannae and became prince of Taranto. He fought the German captain Diepold for years. In June 1205 Diepold ambushed him at Sarno, and he died of his wounds three days later.
